displayQuote: It is true that liberty is precious; so precious that it must be rationed

meta.title: Who really said "It is true that liberty is precious; so precious that it must be rationed"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No known Lenin text contains it. It is reported as hearsay in Sidney & Beatrice Webb's 1935 Soviet Communism: "Lenin is said once to have observed."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is true that liberty is precious; so precious that it must be rationed'?
meta.ogDescription: Not found in Lenin's own works: the line comes secondhand from Sidney & Beatrice Webb's 1935 Soviet Communism, which gives no source for it.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1870–1924 · Russian revolutionary, founder of the Soviet state
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Lenin, and in keeping with his reported view that liberty had to give way to the revolution, but no speech or writing of his is known to contain it. The line appears secondhand in Sidney and Beatrice Webb’s Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation? (first published 1935), where Lenin “is said once to have observed” it. The Webbs give no source.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Sidney & Beatrice Webb (reporting the remark secondhand)
London: Longmans, Green — first published November 1935; text checked in the second impression, February 1936
Vol. 2, ch. XII “The Good Life,” p. 1036

source.excerpt: Lenin is said once to have observed in his epigrammatic way: “It is true that liberty is precious — so precious that it must be rationed”. So long as the available quantum of liberty is not unlimited, the aggregate amount enjoyed within the community is, by appropriate rationing on an equalitarian basis, actually increased.
trail: Wikiquote’s Lenin page lists the line under “Attributions,” citing it “as quoted in” the Webbs’ Soviet Communism: A New Civilization? (1936), not to any work by Lenin. Wikiquote: Vladimir Lenin ↗

The Webbs’ text, vol. 2, p. 1036, gives the line as hearsay: “Lenin is said once to have observed in his epigrammatic way.” The title page of this copy reads “First Published November 1935 / Second Impression February 1936.” Internet Archive full text ↗
The footnote attached to the passage is about British ration cards for sugar during the Great War. It is the Webbs’ own illustration, not a source for Lenin. Internet Archive item ↗
Modern quote sites repeat it with no citation and with altered wording, such as “so precious that it must be carefully rationed.” PastWisdom (marked unverified) ↗
source.cutTag: Hearsay, not a quotation from Lenin
source.excerptNote: The Webbs introduce the line with “is said once to have observed” and cite no speech, text or witness. The footnote at this point is about British wartime sugar ration cards, not about Lenin. Note the Webbs’ dash; the semicolon in the popular form came later.

sourceLink.text: Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation? (1936 impression), full text at the Internet Archive

source.rightsHolder: Estates of Sidney and Beatrice Webb; Longmans, Green & Co. (original publisher) or its successors
source.rightsNote: The English wording is known only from the Webbs’ Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation?, first published in November 1935. Because that work dates from 1931 or later, we treat its text as still in US copyright. No Lenin original, in Russian or in an older translation, is known, so there is no public-domain Lenin source for this line.

author.name: Vladimir Lenin
author.heading: About Vladimir Lenin
author.metaLine: 1870–1924 · Bolshevik leader & first head of the Soviet government
author.bio: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin (born Ulyanov) led the Bolshevik Party to power in the October Revolution of 1917 and headed the Soviet government until his death in 1924. He wrote prolifically, and his speeches, articles and letters fill many volumes of Collected Works. Even so, many of the sharpest lines credited to him come from other people’s memoirs and reports, not from his own texts.

misattribution.heading: How a hearsay epigram became a “Lenin quote”
misattribution.intro: The line is real in the sense that it appears in print in the 1930s. It is not documented as Lenin’s own words, and its wording has kept shifting as it travels.

items.who: Vladimir Lenin, as a direct quotation
items.why: No Lenin speech, article or letter is cited for it anywhere we checked. The only documented source is the Webbs’ report that Lenin “is said once to have observed” it, with no source given. Webb, vol. 2, p. 1036 ↗

items.who: “…so precious that it must be carefully rationed”
items.why: Quote sites add “carefully” and change the Webbs’ dash to a semicolon. One such page labels the quote “unverified” and names no source. The Webbs’ text has neither change. PastWisdom ↗

items.who: “Liberty is precious — so precious that it must be rationed”
items.why: A January 2026 PJ Media opinion piece writes “Lenin once said” and quotes this shortened form, dropping “It is true that.” It gives no source. PJ Media ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The only documented source is Sidney and Beatrice Webb’s Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation? (first published 1935), which passes the line along as something Lenin “is said once to have observed.” We found no Lenin original. Wikiquote lists it as an attribution ↗

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Today the line is quoted as a cynical confession of tyranny. Its earliest known source used it in the opposite spirit. Sidney and Beatrice Webb were Fabian socialists who admired the Soviet experiment; Wikipedia notes that their book drew on publications and statistics supplied by the Soviet embassy in London. They used the epigram approvingly, to argue that when liberty is limited, sharing it out equally “actually increased” the total freedom a community enjoys. Their footnote compares it to British wartime sugar ration cards, which the poor valued because they guaranteed a share. Beatrice Webb (Wikipedia) ↗
So whether the remark was ever Lenin’s or not, the passage that preserved it was a defense of rationing, not an admission of it.
detailsBody: The rationing line should not be confused with an earlier report by the anarchist Alexander Berkman. In The Bolshevik Myth (New York: Boni and Liveright, 1925), Berkman recounts a meeting with Lenin and paraphrases him in indirect speech: “Liberty, he said, is a luxury not to be permitted at the present stage of development.” That is a different sentence in a different source. It shows that Lenin was reported to hold such views, but it does not document the “rationed” wording. Berkman, ch. 13 (Marxists Internet Archive) ↗
We found no Quote Investigator article on this line. Wikiquote cites the Webbs’ book (1936) for it and places it among Lenin’s attributions, not among his sourced works.
